chunks: "You're right that a bond wire is thin, around 25 micrometres, and a single one can only handle something like an amp or so before it heats badly or fuses; the exact limit depends on length, material and the package.
The way you reconcile it is mostly with parallelism and geometry. First, use many wires in parallel.
Six 25 micron gold wires of 3 millimetres each have about 25 milliohms in parallel instead of 150, and each only carries a sixth of the current, so the heating per wire drops with the square.
Power and ground pins are usually bonded with several wires to several pads. Second, shorten the wires and put the die close to the lead.
Third, use bigger conductors where needed: copper or aluminum wire, fat aluminum wire of hundreds of micrometres on power modules, ribbons, or a solid copper clip instead of wires on power MOSFETs.
And for the highest current and best thermals, flip-chip bumps or copper pillars spread the current over an area array.
I'd also mention that on a vertical power MOSFET, the drain current goes through the die backside, so only the source needs these big connections.
What I'd watch for is current sharing, because wires of different length and layout don't share equally, and if one lifts, the others pick up the current."
